subject: Biology
description: Neuron, synapse, neurotransmitters, reflexes, autonomic NS, common disorders

questions.stem: The basic functional unit of the nervous system is the:
questions.explanation: Neuron — basic functional unit. Components: cell body (soma), dendrites (receive), axon (conduct), axon terminals (transmit at synapse). Long projections; longest neuron in human body — sciatic nerve fibre (~1 m). Three types: SENSORY (afferent — carry signals to CNS), MOTOR (efferent — carry to effectors), INTERNEURONS (within CNS, link sensory + motor). Glial cells (Schwann, oligodendrocyte, astrocyte, microglia) — support cells, ~10× more numerous than neurons; form the myelin sheath. Nephron — kidney unit. Erythrocyte — RBC.

questions.stem: The signal between two neurons is transmitted across a tiny gap called a synapse via:

options.option_text: Chemical neurotransmitters released from the axon terminal

questions.explanation: Chemical synapse — the action potential reaches the axon terminal → opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → vesicles release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft (~20 nm wide) → bind to receptors on postsynaptic membrane → trigger new action potential or inhibit. Major neurotransmitters: ACETYLCHOLINE (neuromuscular junction, parasympathetic NS); DOPAMINE (reward, motor — Parkinson's = dopamine deficit); SEROTONIN (mood — SSRIs treat depression); GABA (main inhibitory); GLUTAMATE (main excitatory); NORADRENALINE (sympathetic, alertness). Some synapses are electrical (gap junctions, fast, found in heart and a few brain regions), but the vast majority are chemical.

questions.stem: The reflex action of pulling the hand away from a hot object is mediated by a 'reflex arc' that is processed in the:

options.option_text: Spinal cord (without conscious processing in the brain)

questions.explanation: Reflex arc — fastest path: stimulus → receptor → afferent (sensory) neuron → interneuron in spinal cord → efferent (motor) neuron → effector (muscle). The brain is informed only AFTER the action — that's why you yank your hand back BEFORE feeling the pain. Examples: knee-jerk (patellar reflex — tests stretch reflex; only TWO neurons, no interneuron); withdrawal reflex; corneal reflex; pupillary light reflex. Cerebrum — voluntary action + thinking. Cerebellum — balance, coordination. Hypothalamus — homeostasis (temperature, hunger, thirst, hormones).

questions.stem: Parkinson's disease is associated with the deficiency of which neurotransmitter in the brain?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's — progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra (a midbrain nucleus). Symptoms: TRAP — Tremor (resting), Rigidity, Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural instability. Treatment: L-DOPA (levodopa, crosses blood-brain barrier, converted to dopamine by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase) + carbidopa (peripheral inhibitor). Other neurotransmitter-disease links: Alzheimer's — acetylcholine deficit (treated with cholinesterase inhibitors like donepezil); depression — serotonin/noradrenaline deficit (SSRIs); Huntington's — GABA deficit (genetic, autosomal dominant CAG repeat); Schizophrenia — dopamine excess (antipsychotics block D2 receptors).

questions.stem: The sympathetic nervous system, which prepares the body for 'fight or flight', is part of the:
questions.explanation: Nervous system divisions: CNS (Central — brain + spinal cord); PNS (Peripheral — all nerves outside). PNS divides into SOMATIC (voluntary, skeletal-muscle control) + AUTONOMIC (involuntary). ANS divides into SYMPATHETIC ('fight or flight' — increases heart rate, BP, dilates pupils, suspends digestion; thoracolumbar origin; main neurotransmitter noradrenaline) + PARASYMPATHETIC ('rest and digest' — opposite; craniosacral origin; acetylcholine) + ENTERIC (gut — 'second brain', ~500 million neurons, largely autonomous). Adrenaline (from adrenal medulla) reinforces the sympathetic response.

questions.stem: The myelin sheath that insulates many vertebrate axons and speeds up nerve impulse conduction is formed by:

options.option_text: Schwann cells (in the PNS) and oligodendrocytes (in the CNS)

questions.explanation: Myelin — fatty insulator wrapped around axons. Formed by: (1) Schwann cells in peripheral nervous system — one Schwann cell wraps a single axon segment; (2) Oligodendrocytes in the CNS — one cell can wrap multiple axons. Gaps between myelin segments — Nodes of Ranvier; allow saltatory conduction (impulse 'jumps' from node to node, ~100× faster than continuous conduction). Demyelinating diseases: MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS (CNS, autoimmune attack on myelin — symptoms wax and wane); GUILLAIN-BARRÉ syndrome (PNS, often post-viral, ascending paralysis).

questions.stem: Which of these cranial nerves is the longest, controls many internal organs (gut, heart, lungs) and is the primary nerve of the parasympathetic system?
questions.explanation: Vagus nerve (10th cranial, X) — Latin 'wandering'. Longest cranial nerve; runs from brainstem through the neck and chest into the abdomen. Carries ~75% of all parasympathetic fibres. Slows heart rate, stimulates digestion, regulates breathing. Vagal nerve stimulation (VNS) — therapy for refractory epilepsy and depression. Mnemonic for 12 cranial nerves (I-XII): 'On Old Olympus' Towering Tops, A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops' = Olfactory, Optic, Oculomotor, Trochlear, Trigeminal, Abducens, Facial, Auditory (Vestibulocochlear), Glossopharyngeal, Vagus, Spinal Accessory, Hypoglossal.
